narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. Eclipsing binaries are pairs of stars orbiting each other; we see them because one star passes in front of the other from our perspective, dimming the light we receive. The pipeline starts with over 14,000 target stars, applies statistical checks to light-curve quality and eclipse-like features, compares results against six known variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and then runs an automated pixel-level check to verify that the signal comes from the target star and not from nearby sources. Currently, 212 candidates have passed this full vetting process. To improve reliability, we trained a machine-learning model on 2,159 labeled examples; it outperforms our rule-based baseline. All candidates carry individual caveats and remain research-grade: being listed here means the signal is real and on-target, but does not constitute scientific confirmation by external observers.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other. From Earth's vantage point, one star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. This causes a regular dip in brightness that we can measure in a light curve. Eclipsing binaries are valuable for astronomy because we can infer stellar properties from the depth and shape of these eclipses.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is any star that passes our statistical checks and shows no match in known catalogs. 'Confirmed' is Star Vetter's specific term for a candidate that has also passed an automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself rather than from contaminating nearby sources. Confirmed candidates are still research-grade results and have not undergone external scientific verification.

faqs.question: What is the machine-learning score I see on some candidates?
faqs.answer: It is a secondary score trained on 2,159 labeled examples. It outperforms our rule-based pipeline at distinguishing real eclipsing binaries from false positives. It is provided as additional context only; it does not gate which candidates are pixel-checked or listed on the site. Its purpose is to offer a second opinion, not to make vetting decisions.

faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check whether a candidate is real?
faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This scan compares the brightness dip in the light curve against the spatial brightness distribution around the target star in TESS images, confirming that the eclipse signal originates from the target and not from a nearby star. This is a fully automated process with no manual review as part of the pipeline itself.

faqs.question: What happens if the eclipse period looks ambiguous or aliased?
faqs.answer: We run an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the eclipse depths at odd-numbered cycles against even-numbered cycles. If they differ significantly, the period may be aliased (a half-period or harmonic misidentification). These candidates are flagged with a caveat on their individual pages so users are aware of the ambiguity.

faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate links to its light curve and basic measurements (orbital period and relative eclipse depths). You can download TESS data yourself and examine the signal. Note that deriving stellar masses would require radial-velocity spectroscopy, which this project does not perform; the pipeline measures only orbital period and eclipse depths from the light curve.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?
faqs.answer: Being listed on this site is the endpoint of Star Vetter's pipeline. The candidates are publicly available for follow-up by other researchers, but the vetting pipeline itself does not perform further observations, submit results to catalogs, or track external use. Any professional follow-up, spectroscopy, or scientific confirmation would be conducted independently of this project.
